lesson.title: Down the Gradient: The Physics Behind Diffusion
lesson.summary: Diffusion is the net movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, driven purely by random molecular motion, and it is the mechanism behind everything from a cell absorbing oxygen to a scent spreading across a room.
lesson.body:
Diffusion is the clearest, most direct example of the passive transport introduced in the previous chapter. It is defined as the net movement of particles, whether molecules or ions, from a region where they are more concentrated to a region where they are less concentrated, continuing until the concentration is roughly equal throughout the available space. No membrane is strictly required for diffusion to happen at all, since it also occurs in open air or in a beaker of liquid, but in a biological context diffusion very often refers specifically to movement across the plasma membrane described in earlier chapters.

The underlying cause is simple: individual molecules are always moving randomly due to their own thermal energy, colliding and bouncing in every direction with no preference. In a crowded region, more molecules happen to be bouncing away from that crowd than are bouncing into it, purely because there are more molecules there to begin with, and in a sparse region the reverse is less true. The result, summed across huge numbers of individual random collisions, is a predictable net drift from high concentration toward low concentration, even though each individual molecule's path is completely random and unpredictable.

It is worth being precise about what happens once concentrations equalize. Diffusion does not stop the molecules from moving; thermal motion never stops as long as temperature is above absolute zero. What stops is the net movement, since molecules now cross in both directions at equal rates, a condition called dynamic equilibrium. This distinction matters for understanding why a cell at equilibrium with its environment for some substance is not a dead or inactive cell, just one where that particular substance is no longer changing in net concentration.

Several factors affect how fast diffusion proceeds. A steeper concentration gradient, meaning a bigger difference in concentration between the two regions, produces faster net diffusion. Higher temperature speeds up the random thermal motion of every molecule involved, which speeds diffusion as well. Smaller molecules diffuse faster than larger ones, since they move through their surroundings with less resistance. And, connecting back to the surface-area-to-volume chapter earlier in this unit, a larger membrane surface area allows more total diffusion to occur per unit of time, which is exactly why cells with high exchange needs, such as those lining the lungs or the intestine, often have membrane surfaces that are folded or extended to maximize area.

A concrete, biologically important example is gas exchange in the lungs. Air in the tiny alveolar sacs of the lungs contains a higher concentration of oxygen than the blood flowing through the surrounding capillaries, so oxygen diffuses from the alveolar air across a thin layer of cells into the blood. Carbon dioxide, produced as a waste product of cellular respiration, is more concentrated in the blood than in the alveolar air, so it diffuses in the opposite direction, out of the blood and into the lungs to be exhaled. Both movements happen passively, following the same concentration gradient logic covered in this chapter, with no cellular energy spent moving either gas.
